newsitem.title: USA: Orange County treasurer exceeded guidelines.
newsitem.headline: Orange County treasurer exceeded guidelines.

text.p: Orange County, California's treasurer exceeded some of the county's own investment guidelines, county officials said on Thursday.
Treasurer John Moorlach said state code was never violated, adding that the county's investment guidelines may be too rigid and in need of review.
"The county hasn't suffered," said Moorlach, who assumed the treasurer and tax collector post after the county's unprecedented bankruptcy filing in 1994.
Gary Burton, assistant Orange County chief executive officer, described the violations as minor.
"I don't think that these were serious violations," Burton said. "What happened in Orange County isn't going to happen again."

According to a recent review of county investments, Moorlach invested in firms that lacked long-term credit ratings in violation of the county's guidelines. Of this specific violation, Burton said: "I don't think there's a major problem."
The investments controlled by Moorlach contained some securities that had longer maturities than allowed under county guidelines, Burton said.

In addition, between 5 percent and 10 percent of the funds were invested through one issuer. While in compliance with the county guidelines, the Securities and Exchange Commission recommends up to 5 percent, county officials said.
Burton and Moorlach played down the problems. Moorlach said they were technical and minor breaks with the guidelines.
In August, at the time of the investment review, Moorlach said he was overseeing $300 million of the $1.5 billion county investment pool. The rest was invested by Salomon Brothers.

The investment guidelines were put in place in response to Orange County's bankruptcy in late 1994. The county declared bankruptcy after sustaining investment losses of more than $1.6 billion. The county emerged from bankruptcy in June.
